scenes.text: Syllabus four point four solve simple problems which may be modelled as the motion of connected particles. the end, you can distinguish motion from acceleration. Choose the body and its forces. And calculate reaction and cable tension.

scenes.title: Picture the whole journey

beats.text: Consider a passenger standing inside a lift. The lift carries her upwards towards the next floor.
For a while, it travels steadily upwards. The passenger stays in contact with the floor.
As the lift approaches its destination, it slows down. It still moves upwards, but covers less height each moment.
Finally, it stops. We will study just that braking part, and find the forces that support the passenger and lift.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The lift has mass four hundred kilograms, and the passenger has mass sixty kilograms.
At the start of braking, they move upwards at four metres per second.
They slow uniformly to rest in two seconds.
Take g as ten metres per second squared. The passenger remains in contact with the floor.
The cable stays taut. Ignore other external vertical forces. Take upwards as positive.
Find their acceleration, the upward floor reaction on the passenger, and the cable tension. All three belong to the same braking interval.

scenes.title: First, find the acceleration

beats.text: Up is positive. Both bodies share the same acceleration because the passenger stays on the lift floor.
For constant acceleration, final velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times time.
Substitute: zero equals four plus a times two.
Subtract four from both sides, giving negative four equals two a.
Divide by two. The acceleration is negative two metres per second squared.
The minus sign means downwards. Each second, the upward velocity decreases. Downward acceleration does not mean the lift is moving down.

scenes.title: Forces on the passenger

beats.text: Now isolate the passenger. The floor pushes upwards with reaction R. Gravity pulls downwards with weight m g. Cable tension does not act directly on her.
Newton’s second law says resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Resolve upwards: reaction minus weight equals mass times acceleration.
Use mass sixty, g ten, and acceleration negative two.
So R minus six hundred equals negative one hundred and twenty.
Add six hundred to both sides. The reaction is four hundred and eighty newtons upwards.
The upward reaction is smaller than the downward weight. That imbalance produces the downward acceleration while she travels up.

scenes.title: Forces on the combined system

beats.text: To find cable tension, choose the lift and passenger together. The cable pulls this whole system upwards. Both weights act downwards.
The floor pushes the passenger up, and she pushes the floor down equally. Both are inside our boundary, so their reaction forces cancel in the combined equation.
Again, resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Tension minus total weight equals total mass times acceleration.
Total mass is four hundred plus sixty, giving four hundred and sixty kilograms.
Substitute total mass four hundred and sixty, g ten, and acceleration negative two.
T minus four thousand six hundred equals negative nine hundred and twenty.
Add four thousand six hundred. The cable tension is three thousand six hundred and eighty newtons, upwards.

scenes.title: What changes at constant velocity?

beats.text: Now change the condition: the same lift travels upwards at constant velocity. Is its acceleration still downwards? Take a moment.
No. Constant velocity means zero acceleration. The forces on each chosen body now balance.
For the passenger, R minus m g equals zero, so reaction equals her weight.
For the combined system, tension equals the total weight.
What if the lift speeds up upwards instead? The acceleration is upwards, so each supporting force must exceed the weight it supports.

scenes.title: Choose the body, then apply the law

beats.text: If you choose just the lift, include its own weight and the passenger’s downward reaction. That reaction is external to the lift alone.
Upwards, tension minus the lift’s weight minus reaction equals the lift’s mass times acceleration.
Distinguish motion from acceleration.
